Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/EPA Australian ball tampering Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction
 Jonathan Horn Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle
 Thu 19 Nov 2026 18.35 EST Last modified on Thu 19 Nov 2026 20.31 EST Share W ho said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled.
 Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction.
 An outsider’s view of Australian cricket’s civil war: conflicting ‘truths’ and Cummins in a corner | Ali Martin Read more For many, and certainly for Pat Cummins, his press conference less than a week earlier was supposed to be the final word . Some cricketers write books, some pen essays, and some post videos from the foot of the Himalayas . Some people crumble in front of the baying pack, and some relish it. Daniel Andrews was always more comfortable seeing off two dozen reporters in a Test match-like press conference than facing a hostile radio or current affairs host.
 There may have been more journalists at Cummins’ press conference than there were spectators at the Durban Test. The Australia captain was disarming and indefatigable and won rave reviews. He was praised for his “Churchillian strength”. “Cummins’ press conference was one of the most impressive I’ve seen in public life,” was one take. Another likened him to “a polished private school captain”. The contrast with Khawaja’s interview with Sarah Ferguson on ABC’s 7.30 Report a few nights earlier was stark. Khawaja immediately cancelled any media appearance that wasn’t going to promise half volleys, and public opinion tilted further towards Team Pat.
 View image in fullscreen Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg and interim chair David Boon announce a ball-tampering ‘forum’ during a press conference in Hobart. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images Therein lies the problem with this ongoing saga, and so many others we see in Australian sport. There is a desperate need for a definitive version of events, for smoking guns, for irrefutable evidence. In the absence of any of these, it’s often turned into an examination of character. This is assessed in a number of ways – how good a speaker you are, your relationship with journalists, your skin colour, how good a bloke you’re deemed to be, even what state you play for.
 We pinpoint the villain, the schemer, the bagman, the sacrificial lamb, the cleanskin, the whistleblower. But because this story never rests, and because cricketers have more platforms than Greg Louganis, this perception shifts from hour to hour, from press conference to podcast. The sportsman who’s “Churchillian” one minute can look and sound like Mark Latham a week later.
 Right or wrong. Unimpeachable or unreliable. A coronial inquest or an anonymous forum. Black or white. But if there’s one thing that recent sporting scandals have demonstrated, the truth often lurks somewhere in the grey . Whether you think this was a carefully orchestrated scheme that everybody was in up to their ears or a harebrained plot involving a sneaky few, the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle.
 It brings to mind something cricket reporter Peter Lalor talked about on his podcast Cricket Et Al recently – that Cummins is actually an incurious person, the sort of sportsman who narrows his focus to what he needs to worry about. Some athletes need to know the ins and outs of a duck’s bum. Some, like Steve Smith and perhaps Cummins’, put their hands to their ears and cry “I don’t want to know about it!” giving them legal and ethical wriggle room when they’re batting away journalists or integrity officers.
 View image in fullscreen Usman Khawaja and David Warner speak on Kayo Cricket during the third ODI between Australia and England in Hobart. Photograph: Steve Bell/Getty Images Sporting scandals these days so often become runaway trains. They often follow a familiar trajectory – the sense of all hell breaking loose for the first 48 hours, the splinter into the usual culture war arguments, and the gradual pressure release through leaks, backgrounding and – occasionally – facts. We saw that with the recent controversy involving the Sydney Swans at the Pullman Hotel. Within hours, it had invited comment from the prime minister, the governor general and personal injury lawyers.

 Like “sandpapergate”, the AFL saga was a story that was followed closely by people who normally don’t concern themselves with sport. But unlike the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, there was a sophisticated PR and media management infrastructure that was able to put the brakes on the story. News that Victoria police had decided not to charge the four Swans players being investigated dropped while Cummins’ was into the second hour of his press conference, and during a global Microsoft Outlook outage.
 Likewise, for a few days in August, it seemed as though the Geelong concussion waiver scandal had the potential to bring down some of the most prominent figures in football, and change the way we look at head trauma. But then, nothing. It was textbook crisis management from both the club and the league. Some of the AFL’s most senior staff have worked at the highest levels of state and federal governments. They’ve worked in prime minister’s offices and on state election campaigns. They made that story go away.
 Shame is the only punishment in Australian cricket’s sandpaper scandal | Geoff Lemon Read more This is not to commend the AFL in any way. We should be more concerned that a large organisation can put a story like that to sleep than another that lets a relative trifle fester away for eight years. But it hammers home the central frustration of sandpapergate. This story should never have been allowed to get as big as it did. Nothing about the reaction, the response and the reprisals have been proportional.
 That goes well beyond the administrators. If prime ministers are going to concern themselves with sporting controversies they should start with gambling and work backwards from there. If pundits are going to describe this as Australian cricket’s “JFK moment”, and call for coronial-like inquests in search of an incontrovertible “truth”, they are ignoring the realities of dressing rooms, of human frailty, even of memory. If a story like sandpapergate breaks again in sport, the response from those who administer it, play it and comment on it needs to have some sort of perspective. Otherwise, we live in an age where these stories chase their own arse for years – a rolling loop of outrage, of judgment and of overreaction.
